newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia thinktank sees healthy '98 growth.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia thinktank sees healthy '98 growth.

text.p: The Commonwealth Games will help Malaysia's economic growth surge again in 1998 after two years of a government-engineered slowdown, a state-backed think tank said on Tuesday.

The country's gross domestic product (GDP) growth will ease to 8.3 percent in 1996 and 8.2 percent next year before recovering to 8.5 percent in 1998, the Malaysian Institute of Economic Research (MIER) said in its economic outlook report.
MIER said the growth would pick up in 1998 "when Malaysia plays host to the Commonwealth Games".
"Economic growth will be spurred by strong private sector expenditure growth," the report said.
The Commonwealth Games are expected to increase the already heavy economic activity in the country, one Kuala Lumpur-based economist said.
A large number of projects, like the new Kuala Lumpur International Airport and other infrastructure projects related to the games are expected to be completed in 1998.
Economists say even without the games, GDP growth would remain around 8.0 percent because of other infrastructure programmes.
In 1995, Malaysia registered annual GDP growth of 9.5 percent, with the economic pace estimated by the government to fall to 8.2 percent this year and 8.0 percent in 1997.
In a Reuters poll on Monday, 16 large research houses forecast average GDP growth of 8.08 percent in 1996 and 7.99 percent next year.
Tighter monetary policy, lower government spending and a downturn in the electronics sector have moderated growth in the current year, the MIER report said.

The report, issued as part of a two-day outlook conference, also forecast that the current account deficit as a percentage of nominal gross national product (GNP) "will moderate" to 4.7 percent in 1997 and 4.2 percent in 1998.
It said the improvement in the current account gap would be due to "the expected improvement in the trade balance".
The government has estimated the current account of the balance of payments at 6.3 percent of GNP in 1996, against nine percent of GNP in 1995.
The inflation rate is expected to be 3.7 percent in 1997, and 3.8 percent the following year, the MIER report said.
Inflation, as measured by the Consumer Price Index, was 3.4 percent in 1995. It is estimated by the government to be 3.6 percent in 1996 and 3.5 percent next year.
"People who were comparing Malaysia with Mexico last year will not have much to say after such good figures," said an economist with a Singapore-based research house.
A high current account deficit last year forced Mexico to devalue its currency, triggering an international crisis. Many had feared a similar meltdown in Malaysia.
MIER said domestic interest rates are expected to stay firm for the rest of this year and in the first half of 1997.

It said firm interest rates are needed "to contain inflationary pressure as loans growth is still very strong and the growth rate of money supply, although moderating, is still above levels consistent with price stability".
It forecast the three-month interbank offered rate at 7.2-7.4 percent in the first quarter of 1997. On Tuesday, the three-month rate was quoted at 7.35/7.40 percent.

In the Reuters poll, economists forecast that the benchmark three-month Kuala Lumpur interbank offered rate (KLIBOR) will fall to 6.9 percent by the end of 1997. The decline would be gradual with the three-month KLIBOR at an average 7.21 percent at the end of the first quarter of 1997, the poll said.
($1=2.52 ringgit)
